sections.html:
• Family: Cyprinidae
  • Origin: White Cloud Mountains of China
  • Adult size: 4 cm (1.5 inches)
  • Life expectancy: 3 to 5 years
  • Social: peaceful and sociable
  • Tank level: top to middle
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres (10 gallons)
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Breeding: egg scatterers; easy to breed
  • Care: easy; good fish for beginners
  • pH 6.0 to 8.0
  • Hardness: 5 to 19 dGH
  • Temperature: 15 to 22°C (60 to 72°F)

The geographic origins of this fish in China and Vietnam have undergone significant changes, which have negatively impacted its habitat, and slowly the species has disappeared. Beginning in 1980, Tanichthys albonubes had not been seen in nature, leading to the belief that it had become extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number of native populations have been discovered in isolated locations within the coastal provinces of Guangdong and Hainan Island in China, as well as in Quảng Ninh province in Vietnam. The species is still very rare in the wild and is considered endangered in China. Efforts are underway to reintroduce captive-bred populations into the wild, but currently all white cloud mountain minnows sold in the aquarium trade are captive-bred.

When kept in the right temperature range, this fish is very hardy and well suited for beginner hobbyists. Although undemanding when it comes to water quality, it does not deal with heat well. There is evidence that keeping white cloud mountain minnows in water constantly above 22°C (72°F) will shorten their lifespan.

White cloud mountain minnows are sometimes kept as pond fish to help control mosquito breeding. They cannot be kept with large pond fish, as they will be eaten. They do make good companions for African dwarf frogs. While they tolerate cool water, they cannot be left in outdoor ponds in winter in areas where the water freezes.
Water hardness and pH are not critical, but it is wise to avoid extremes. Avoid all medications containing copper, as white cloud mountain minnows are very sensitive to copper.

The substrate should be fine and darker in color, with plenty of vegetation as well as some rocks and driftwood. Leave an open area for swimming and offer subdued lighting to bring out the colors of this fish.

White cloud mountain minnows eat all types of food, including live, frozen and flake food. In their native habitat, they are voracious insect eaters. They particularly relish mosquito larvae, daphnia and brine shrimp. Feed a good variety of dry and frozen foods, including live foods whenever possible.

White cloud mountain minnows should be kept in good-sized schools, preferably of half a dozen or more. When kept singly, they tend to lose color and hide most of the time. They are peaceful and fit well with other small peaceful fish. Avoid larger tankmates, as they will be inclined to eat white cloud mountain minnows. The same is true of any aggressive species.

They are often sold as companions for goldfish, as both prefer cooler water. However, goldfish can and often do eat fish the size of white clouds, so combining these two species in the same aquarium is not a good idea.
Sexual differences are slight, and determining the gender accurately can be difficult. Males are more slender and brilliantly colored than females. Females ready to spawn have a fuller abdomen.

White clouds reach sexual maturity between 6 months and 1 year of age. When mature enough to spawn, males display against each other, spreading their fins and showing their most vibrant colors to attract a female.

They are easy to breed and a good choice for first-time breeders. They are egg scatterers that breed year-round. The pair provides no parental care.

There are two approaches. One is to keep a large school of white clouds (and only white clouds) in their original tank and let them breed there. Because these fish are not as aggressive about eating their eggs and fry as other fish, some young will survive if there are plants and other hiding places near the bottom.

Another option is a small breeding tank of 20 to 40 litres (5 to 10 gallons) with a couple of the most colorful males and twice as many females. Equip it with a spawning mop and/or clumps of plants where the fish can deposit eggs. For spawning, the water should be soft, with pH 6.5 to 7.5 and a temperature of 20 to 22°C (68 to 72°F). No substrate is necessary in a separate breeding tank. Gentle filtration, such as a sponge filter, is recommended.

Either way, condition the fish with live foods before spawning, particularly brine shrimp, daphnia and mosquito larvae. High-quality frozen foods can be used if live food is unavailable.

Once spawning begins, eggs are scattered over the plants or spawning mop for up to 24 hours. The eggs hatch in 36 to 48 hours. Remove the parents once the eggs begin to hatch. Fry should initially be fed very fine micro-foods or liquid fry food, followed by freshly hatched brine shrimp. The young grow rapidly and are easy to care for.

White cloud mountain minnows are small, colorful fish, once termed "the working man's neon" because they were similar to neon tetras in color but were not as expensive.

For over half a century the white cloud mountain minnow (Tanichthys albonubes) was the only species in the genus. However, in 2001, two additional species found in Vietnam were recognized: Tanichthys micagemmae and Tanichthys thacbaensis. Of those two, only Tanichthys micagemmae (Vietnamese white cloud) is available in the aquarium trade.

The mouth slants upward, with the lower jaw slightly protruding. They possess no barbels, and the dorsal fin is positioned past the mid-line of the body, in line with the anal fin. The body is a shimmering bronze-brown, with a fluorescent line running from eye to tail, where it ends in a dark spot surrounded by brilliant red. The belly is whiter than the body, and the anal and dorsal fins are both splashed with red and edged in white. Several color variations exist, including a golden variety as well as a long-finned variant known as the meteor minnow.
